records.sourceFile: Redefining the draft pick valuation in the National Football League.pdf

paper.citation: Hadley B, Kim JW, Magnusen M, Kim KT. Redefining the draft pick valuation in the National Football League. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2025;7:1628223.
paper.abstract: Regression models of 1993 to 2012 draft picks suggest late-round picks are undervalued by Jimmy Johnson's Pick Value Chart, and first-round trade-ups are associated with lower career wAV, games played and seasons started. The authors report a recalibrated pick value chart and a Day 3 emphasis.
paper.tldr: Late-round NFL picks produced more career value than the classic pick value chart predicts, and first-round trade-ups were linked to weaker player outcomes. Front offices may want to test these findings against their own draft records before changing how they trade picks.
paper.methods: Archival data from pro-football-reference.com for 4,996 draft picks from 1993 to 2012. Model 1 averaged each of 262 pick slots and fitted fifth-order polynomial regressions to wAV, GP and ST. Model 2 used player-level data with seven round-specific trade-up dummies. The results are from ordinary regression with the outcome measures as reported on the source site.
paper.findings: Model 1 R2 was 0.90 for wAV, 0.82 for GP and 0.90 for ST. The last first-round pick was valued at about 56% of the first pick on GP, versus 20% on the chart. In Model 2, first-round trade-ups had significantly lower wAV (coefficient -5.44, P = .013), GP (-13.33, P = .018) and ST (-0.82, P = .008). Round 4 trade-ups had a significant positive effect on ST (0.92, P = .011), and other rounds were not significant. Model 2 R2 was 0.31 for wAV, 0.22 for GP and 0.31 for ST.
paper.limitations: Outcomes are career totals from a single league, and the models do not adjust for position, team, injuries, or contract status. Model 2 explains little variance, and the round-specific effects are inconsistent (only Round 1 and Round 4 reach significance, with Round 4 effects visible only on ST). The paper does not test whether a recalibrated chart improves real draft results. The authors note that financial constraints can also shape draft behaviour.
paper.practicalImplications: Draft boards may want to give more weight to later-round picks than the classic chart does, and first-round trade-ups should be checked against the lower average outcomes reported here. These are average patterns across the league, so each draft decision still needs player-level evaluation.
paper.athleteDev: The paper gives no development or training data. Its relevance is to how teams value young players drafted from college and how they assess career output across positions.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study does not examine injury, rehabilitation or return to play.

records.sourceFile: Relationship Between Preseason Training Load and In-Season Availability in Elite Australian Football Players.pdf

paper.citation: Murray NB, Gabbett TJ, Townshend AD. Relationship Between Preseason Training Load and In-Season Availability in Elite Australian Football Players. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2017;12(6):749-755.
paper.abstract: In 46 elite male AFL players from one club, the share of preseason sessions completed was linked to higher GPS training loads, more in-season training and match availability, and lower injury rates that were not statistically significant. Players who completed less than half of preseason training had the highest injury rate (26.8 per 1000 h versus 14.2 in the high-completion group).
paper.tldr: Elite AFL players who completed more of their preseason training carried higher training loads into the season and played a larger share of matches. The availability and injury differences were not statistically significant, and low-completion players had spent much more of preseason in rehabilitation, so completion is a useful monitoring signal rather than a proven cause.
paper.methods: Single-cohort observational study of 46 male AFL players. Players were grouped by the percentage of main preseason sessions completed (high >85%, medium 50 to 84.9%, low <50%). A 10-Hz GPS unit with accelerometer recorded total, low, moderate, high and very-high-speed distance and player load in training and matches. Injuries that caused a missed match were logged by club medical staff and expressed per 1000 h. Group and phase effects were analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, magnitude-based inferences and chi-square tests.
paper.findings: Preseason training loads were about 1.3 times higher than in-season (P=.02). In the first half of the season, high and medium groups covered significantly more total distance (P=.03 and P=.02) and had higher player load (P=.03 and P=.02) than the low group. Match availability was 76.7% (high), 76.1% (medium) and 52.7% (low); these differences were not statistically significant (P>.05) but were rated very likely meaningful by magnitude-based inference. Injury rates were 14.2, 17.7 and 26.8 per 1000 h, a difference that was not significant (chi-square=3.48, P=.17), across 50 in-season injuries.
paper.limitations: Data come from one club and one season with 50 injuries, which limits power and generalizability. Groups were not randomized, and low-completion players spent far more of the preseason in rehabilitation, so causation cannot be inferred. Internal load was not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: Strength and conditioning staff can use preseason completion as a monitoring signal, since players who completed less preseason training had lower in-season loads and fewer match appearances. Strategies that keep players in the main program during preseason, rather than in rehabilitation or modified sessions, are the practical target.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: players who completed more of the planned preseason program had higher GPS distance and player load in the first half of the season and a higher share of matches played, so preseason completion is worth tracking as an early marker of in-season load capacity. The design cannot separate the effect of training completed from the injury or rehabilitation status that limited it.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the study does not measure return-to-play criteria or rehabilitation outcomes. Because the low-completion group had far more rehabilitation time, it cannot be used to set return-to-play timelines.

records.sourceFile: Relationships between lower limb muscle characteristics and force-velocity profiles derived during sprinting and jumping.pdf

paper.citation: Bellinger P, Bourne MN, Duhig S, Lievens E, Kennedy B, Martin A, et al. Relationships between Lower Limb Muscle Characteristics and Force-Velocity Profiles Derived during Sprinting and Jumping. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021;53(7):1400-1411.
paper.abstract: In 19 subelite male rugby league players, estimated muscle fibre type and specific muscle volumes explained much of the variation in maximal power, force and velocity derived from jumping and sprinting force-velocity profiles.
paper.tldr: Estimated fibre type and the size of key thigh muscles were associated with maximal power, force and velocity in jumping and sprinting in these players. This is a cross-sectional association, not a training result.
paper.methods: Nineteen subelite male rugby league players performed loaded and unloaded squat jumps and two 30 m sprints to derive vertical and horizontal force-velocity-power profiles. Fascicle length, pennation angle and thickness were measured with B-mode ultrasound, muscle volumes with MRI, and gastrocnemius medialis fibre typology estimated from carnosine with proton MR spectroscopy. Univariable regression screened predictors, then stepwise regression identified the best combinations.
paper.findings: Vertical maximal power was best explained by gastrocnemius fibre typology and vastus lateralis volume (adjusted r2 = 0.440, p = 0.006), and horizontal maximal power by gastrocnemius fibre typology plus adductor and vastus intermedius volume (adjusted r2 = 0.634, p = 0.001). Vertical and horizontal maximal velocity were best explained by gastrocnemius fibre typology (adjusted r2 = 0.580) and fibre typology plus biceps femoris short head volume (0.590), both p < 0.001. Maximal force was explained by rectus femoris and vastus lateralis volume (vertical, r2 = 0.430) and adductor and vastus medialis volume (horizontal, 0.432); architecture explained little variation.
paper.limitations: Small sample of 19 subelite male players, cross-sectional, with many correlations raising type I error risk. Fibre typology was estimated from carnosine in one muscle, and architecture was measured at single sites with extrapolated fascicle length. The abstract lists adductor and vastus medialis volume in the horizontal power model with p = 0.032, whereas the results and Table 4 give adductor and vastus intermedius volume with p = 0.001; this record uses the table.
paper.practicalImplications: Muscle volume and estimated fibre type are associated with jump and sprint force-velocity variables and could be considered when interpreting power profiles in rugby players. Their value for guiding training change has not been tested here.
paper.athleteDev: Specific muscle volumes and estimated fibre type explained much of the variation in jump and sprint power in these players, which supports considering muscle characteristics when interpreting force-velocity profiles, though not as a direct training prescription.
paper.rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It was done in uninjured subelite players and does not test whether muscle characteristics or force-velocity profiles indicate readiness to return after injury.

records.sourceFile: Repeated sprint training - The effects of session volume on acute physiological, neuromuscular, perceptual and performance outcomes in athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Thurlow, F., McLaren, S. J., Townshend, A., Morrison, M., Cowley, N., Weakley, J. Repeated sprint training: The effects of session volume on acute physiological, neuromuscular, perceptual and performance outcomes in athletes. European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;1-13.
paper.abstract: The authors examined how repeated sprint training session volume (set by sprint distance and number of repetitions) affects acute physiological, perceptual, sprint and neuromuscular responses in 14 trained athletes. The 800 m protocol produced the greatest physiological and perceptual demands, while the 200 m protocol produced the lowest. Neuromuscular recovery was unclear, with large inter-individual variation.
paper.tldr: Session volume drives the acute load of repeated sprint training. At 400 m, the sprint distance chosen changes the external load more than the internal load. Coaches can use 200 m sessions to introduce maximal sprinting and 800 m sessions for the largest aerobic stimulus.
paper.methods: Fourteen healthy trained athletes (10 male, 4 female) completed four repeated sprint protocols, each two sets of 10 x 40 m, 5 x 40 m, 10 x 20 m or 5 x 20 m, one per week in a Latin-square crossover design, with 30 s inter-repetition rest and 3 min inter-set rest. Heart rate and oxygen consumption were measured, with differential RPE, session RPE, sprint decrement and GPS acceleration and high-speed sprint distance. Countermovement jump, leg stiffness and isometric hamstring strength were measured before, immediately after, and at 24 and 48 h. Protocols were compared with ANOVA and effect sizes.
paper.findings: The 10 x 40 m protocol (800 m) averaged about 89% of maximal heart rate and 72% of VO2max, had the greatest sprint decrement and time above 90% VO2max (large effects), and had a very large higher session RPE training load than all other protocols; its heart rate exceeded only the 5 x 20 m protocol, and VO2 differences were not definitive. The 5 x 20 m protocol (200 m) had the lowest training load. At 400 m, heart rate, VO2, session RPE load, leg RPE and sprint decrement were similar between 5 x 40 m and 10 x 20 m, and acceleration load was greater with 10 x 20 m (large effect). The 40 m protocols gave over 100 m above 90% of maximal sprint speed per session vs 67 m for 10 x 20 m, though the 5 x 40 m vs 10 x 20 m difference was not reported as definitive. Neuromuscular changes at 0, 24 and 48 h were unclear, with decrement, no change or potentiation across athletes.
paper.limitations: The sample was small (n = 14) and the authors describe the analysis as exploratory. Changing sprint distance also changed work-to-rest ratios, which limits comparisons. The neuromuscular measures were jump, leg stiffness and isometric hamstring tests, and eccentric hamstring function was not measured. Volumes were limited to 200 to 800 m, and the study did not measure training adaptations over time.
paper.practicalImplications: Session volume and sprint distance change acute load in different ways. Practitioners can use 200 m (5 x 20 m) to introduce maximal sprinting and 800 m (10 x 40 m) for the largest acute demand. At 400 m, the authors suggest 5 x 40 m for more high-speed running and 10 x 20 m for more acceleration load. Adding repetitions at a fixed sprint distance did not greatly raise aerobic demand, so longer sprints may be a better way to increase the stimulus.
paper.athleteDev: Use sprint distance and volume to set the acute load of repeated sprint training. Use 200 m at the start of a block, and 400 m with 40 m sprints when maximal running exposure is the goal. Use 800 m when the aim is the highest session demand.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy athletes who had been injury-free for at least 3 months, and it did not include injured or rehabilitating athletes or any return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Repeated sprint training in heat and hypoxia - Acute responses to manipulating exercise to rest ratio.pdf

paper.citation: Dennis, M. C., Goods, P. S. R., Binnie, M. J., Girard, O., Wallman, K. E., Dawson, B., et al. Repeated-sprint training in heat and hypoxia: Acute responses to manipulating exercise-to-rest ratio. European Journal of Sport Science. 2022.
paper.abstract: The authors compared two exercise-to-rest ratios (1:2 and 1:4) during repeated-sprint cycling in hot, hypoxic conditions in 12 male team-sport athletes. The 1:4 ratio gave higher mechanical power and core temperature, while the 1:2 ratio gave greater muscle oxygen extraction, which the authors suggest may be used to target different outcomes.
paper.tldr: In hot, hypoxic conditions, 10 sprints of 5 s with longer rest (1:4) produced slightly more power and a higher core temperature than 5 sprints of 10 s (1:2). The 1:2 format caused more muscle deoxygenation. These are single-session responses, not training effects.
paper.methods: Twelve trained male team-sport athletes completed a familiarisation session and two randomised experimental sessions in an environmental chamber at 40 C, 50% relative humidity and a simulated altitude of about 3000 m (FiO2 0.144). Sessions were 3 sets of 5 x 10 s sprints (1:2, 5 min between sets) or 3 sets of 10 x 5 s sprints (1:4, 2.5 min between sets), matched for sprint and session duration. Mean and peak power, total work, muscle oxygenation (near-infrared spectroscopy), core and skin temperature, heart rate, blood lactate and RPE were recorded. Data were analysed with linear mixed models.
paper.findings: The 1:4 protocol had higher mean power output and total work (both 5.2% higher) and peak power (4.4% higher) than the 1:2 protocol (condition effects p = 0.002 to 0.007). Muscle deoxygenation during sprints was greater with 1:2 (28.2 vs 22.4%, p < 0.001), and minimum muscle oxygenation was lower with 1:2 (p = 0.034). Peak core temperature was higher with 1:4 (38.44 vs 38.20 C, p = 0.028), and session core temperature was also higher with 1:4 (38.10 vs 37.89 C, p < 0.001); neither reached the roughly 38.5 C cited for heat acclimation. RPE was higher with 1:2 throughout the protocol (p = 0.019), and blood lactate rose more with 1:2 (14.5 vs 11.8 mmol/L at end of exercise, interaction p = 0.027). Muscle reoxygenation during recovery, heart rate and sweat loss did not differ between protocols.
paper.limitations: Twelve men were tested once per protocol in one environment with no airflow, and a thermoneutral control was not tested, so the findings may not apply to other conditions, women or other populations. The participants were tier 4 trained athletes under the McKay et al. framework, and the authors note that more highly trained athletes may respond differently. The study measured acute responses only and did not assess training adaptation. Muscle oxygenation came from a single near-infrared site. The trials were conducted in a season when some heat acclimatisation may have been present.
paper.practicalImplications: In hot, hypoxic sprint sessions, a 1:4 exercise-to-rest ratio with 5 s sprints produced more power and a higher core temperature than a 1:2 ratio with 10 s sprints. A 1:2 ratio produced more muscle deoxygenation. Coaches can use the ratio to shape the stimulus, but the study does not show which ratio gives better long-term results.
paper.athleteDev: Use the exercise-to-rest ratio to change the acute stimulus in heat and hypoxia sessions. A 1:4 ratio with short sprints gives more power and a higher core temperature with lower RPE, while 1:2 gives more muscle deoxygenation, higher RPE and more blood lactate.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy trained athletes in a single laboratory session, with no injured or rehabilitating athletes and no return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Resistance training variable manipulations are less relevant  than intrinsic biology in affecting muscle fiber hypertrophy.pdf

paper.citation: Angleri V, Damas F, Phillips SM, et al. Resistance training variable manipulations are less relevant than intrinsic biology in affecting muscle fiber hypertrophy. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2022.
paper.abstract: Twenty resistance-trained men had one leg assigned to standard progressive training and the other to a variable program for 8 weeks. Both legs gained similar muscle fiber size, and individual differences were larger than differences between programs.
paper.tldr: In trained men training to or near failure, changing load, volume, muscle action and rest between sessions did not add fiber growth beyond standard progressive training. Individual differences in fiber growth mattered more than the choice of program.
paper.methods: Twenty resistance-trained young men had each leg randomly assigned to a standard progressive program (RT-CON) or a variable program (RT-VAR) for 8 weeks, two sessions per week. Vastus lateralis biopsies were taken before and after training, and a 17th session was biopsied acutely at 0 and 24 h to assess gene expression.
paper.findings: Type I and II fiber cross-sectional area rose about 12 to 13% in both legs, with no difference between programs. Satellite cell and myonuclei numbers did not change. Most gene expression changes were similar between programs, except a larger acute MyoG increase after RT-VAR, and the between-leg correlation for fiber area change was r = 0.89.
paper.limitations: Baseline biopsy came from one leg only, and histology used 19 of 20 participants. The sample was young resistance-trained men over one 8-week block, and accumulated volume load was 12.6% higher in the variable leg. Gene expression was sampled at limited time points, which the authors note may explain its poor alignment with individual fiber growth.
paper.practicalImplications: For trained lifters training to or near failure, variation in load, volume, muscle action and rest did not add fiber growth over standard progressive loading. Variation may still suit people who find a varied program more motivating, but it should not be expected to change hypertrophy in this population.
paper.athleteDev: Standard progressive loading produced the same fiber growth as the variable scheme in trained men, so variation alone is not a reason to change a hypertrophy program. Individual gains varied widely under both programs, so one program may produce very different results across athletes.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study tested hypertrophy in healthy trained men and cannot inform return to sport, injury rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Review of WADA prohibited substances - Limited evidence for performance-enhancing effects.pdf

paper.citation: Heuberger JAAC, Cohen AF. Review of WADA Prohibited Substances: Limited Evidence for Performance-Enhancing Effects. Sports Med. 2018.
paper.abstract: Review of the evidence for performance enhancement across the 23 substance classes on the 2018 WADA Prohibited List, using PubMed searches. Only 5 of 23 classes showed evidence of enhancing actual sports performance, with growth hormone showing similar evidence only in untrained subjects, and the evidence base is 11 studies with 266 subjects.
paper.tldr: Most of the substances on the WADA Prohibited List have no convincing evidence of improving athletic performance in trained athletes. The few classes with evidence improve strength, sprint or accuracy tasks, and the authors found no studies showing benefit on reliable markers of endurance performance.
paper.methods: Narrative review with a PubMed search using keyword combinations for each substance class, supplemented by reference lists. Evidence was graded by study design (double-blind randomized trials as level 1) and by training status (untrained, trained or highly trained), with actual performance tests preferred over surrogate markers.
paper.findings: Five classes showed evidence of enhancing actual performance in trained subjects: anabolic agents (strength, three studies with 91 volunteers), beta2-agonists (peak sprint power and muscle strength, three studies with 39 volunteers), stimulants (muscle strength, sprint performance and 1500 m run time, 58 trained subjects in Table 1), glucocorticoids (one study with 10 subjects, 11% gain in one-legged hopping force, a surrogate marker) and beta-blockers (13.4% better shooting, one study of 33 subjects). Growth hormone improved sprint performance in untrained subjects only, 11 classes had no well-designed studies, and 6 classes had evidence of no relevant effect.
paper.limitations: The search used PubMed only with keyword combinations, and no formal appraisal or PRISMA reporting is described. The authors note that trials of banned substances in elite athletes are very hard or impossible to run, so the target population is largely missing, and that endurance surrogates such as VO2max have limited predictive value for performance.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who advise athletes on prohibited substances should treat the evidence as limited, and should not assume that a listed substance improves performance in a given sport. The authors note that clear evidence of no effect for a class would be useful to share with athletes, and that research to fill the gaps in the evidence base could be done in many areas.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff should not use this review to judge whether a listed substance helps a specific athlete, since most evidence concerns strength or sprint tasks in small trials. Any discussion of performance-enhancing claims should refer to the specific substance class and the study population.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The review does not address return to sport or injury rehabilitation, and it cannot inform clearance decisions after injury.
